description:
Gideon here, an Electrical and Electronics Engineering student into embedded systems and TinyML. I do debate, so I can lead our pitch.
Our project, CODE-BLUE, warns the crew when an astronaut's health looks wrong, using Edge Impulse and a simple dashboard.
Join us if you want: a beginner-friendly team, and a project for your portfolio.
We need: a web or dashboard builder, a Python and data helper, a designer or storyteller, and anyone with health knowledge.
Beginners are welcome. Message me!
summary:
CODE-BLUE is a software prototype that gives astronauts health alerts even when Earth is too far to help. It reads a heart signal (ECG) and uses a tiny machine-learning model, trained to sort it into three levels: Green (normal), Yellow (unusual), and Red (act now). A dashboard replays the signal like a live device, so we could demo it without hardware.
It addresses the challenge by monitoring astronaut health on the device itself. There is no cloud and no wait for mission control, where a message can take up to twenty minutes each way. The model is small, so it can fit a light, low-power wearable. This matters because every extra pound costs thousands of dollars to launch.
We trained it on synthetic ECG from PhysioNet. Our labels are our own rule, and this is not a medical diagnosis. We used AI tools to help build it.
details:
What it does and how it does it.
CODE-BLUE reads an astronaut's heart signal (ECG) and shows one of three alert levels: Green (normal), Yellow (unusual), Red (act now). We cut real ECG recordings into 2-minute windows at 50 Hz and labeled them normal, elevated, or critical. We trained a small classification model in Edge Impulse using its heart rate and heart rate variability (HR/HRV) processing block. A dashboard replays the model's results like a live device. It has buttons to simulate each level and a "sensor disconnected" test. The hardware is simulated.

The benefits

  • It runs on the device, with no cloud and no wait for Earth.
  • It is small and light, so it avoids the launch cost of heavy equipment.
  • The three colors are easy to read with little training.

The intended impact
To give crews early warning of unusual heart patterns on missions where Mission Control is minutes away. It is a support tool, not a medical diagnosis.

Tools, languages, and hardware

  • Edge Impulse Studio (model training)
  • Python: wfdb, numpy, pandas, scipy (data preparation)
  • Data: PhysioNet Sudden Cardiac Death Holter Database (real ECG), plus synthetic ECG as a backup
  • Dashboard: HTML, CSS, Python, Javascript and Typescript
  • AI tools: Claude helped with planning, and the code
  • Hardware: none. The device is simulated in software.
  • Based on Roni Bandini's open-source Edge Impulse project.

It creativeness
We moved a stress-detection idea into deep-space health with three alert levels. We tied the story to Apollo's slow, by-hand ECG reading and to the payload and delay limits of Mars missions. We also built the device as a software replay, so anyone can test it.

What we considered

  • Mass and launch cost
  • Local processing, because of limits on cloud use
  • Message delay to Earth
  • Ease of use under stress
  • Honesty: our labels are our own rule. The test uses patients the model did not train on. Radiation effects and medical-grade accuracy are not tested, and they are on our roadmap.
  • NASA resources (ARCHeR, Tempus Pro, HRP research) guided our design. Our training data comes from PhysioNet.
